newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada to resume salmon dispute talks -U.S.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada to resume salmon dispute talks -U.S.

text.p: The United States and Canada have agreed to renew negotiations to resolve their salmon dispute, the State Department announced on Wednesday.

"The two governments have agreed on a process of government-to-government negotiations which includes direct participation by stakeholders from relevant regions," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

"Two groups, representing northern and southern fishery interests, will be asked to review key fisheries and make recommendations on fishing arrangements which are consistent with the (Pacific Salmon) treaty principles" with the first meeting expected next week in Portland, Oregon, he said.
Burns said that whether the recommendations are binding or not "depends on the negotiations we're about to have."
But he stressed: "We have confidence that we have broken through a psychological barrier after 12 years and we might make some progress" in resolving the dispute.
Canada and the United States have not been able to agree on implementation of the principles of the Pacific Salmon Treaty, which was signed in 1985.

There had been repeated unsuccessful attempts to reach a solution, including mediation in 1996. Last summer, the governors of the states of Alaska, Washington and Oregon pledged a new political will and called for a new process involving the stakeholders to resolve the conflict.

Burns said that the two groups representing fishery interests would report to the chief negotiators -- Canadian Yves Fortier and American Mary-Beth West -- who are to make a preliminary review of progress by mid-March.
